summary: We developed an interactive lunar outpost simulator designed for two target audiences. For children aged 7 to 12, the simulator is intuitive enough to play and have fun while learning what life is like on a lunar base and discovering what it means to be an astronaut. For astronauts, it accurately recreates real-world mission scenarios, allowing them to practice and train. This dual approach is impactful because both groups benefit: children can explore STEM careers and inspire their future vocations, while astronauts reinforce mission readiness by experiencing the real consequences of their decisions.
details:
It works with a web page that visualizes the camera where the astronaut makes decisions and manages data. There, various problems will arise that they will have to solve within a set time limit, managing their radiation levels and energy, and performing constant maintenance. In addition, it offers an interactive experience so that children who try it can discover what it would be like to live on Mars, and provides astronauts with a tool to practice, learn about potential risk situations, and get an idea of how to solve them. With this, we aim to have an impact so that children can easily understand how complex it can be to be at an outpost on Mars. It is creative, implements real NASA data, and translates it simply into a game. And the tools we used were: Languages: TypeScript (application logic), TSX/JSX (UI), CSS (custom animations and effects), JSON (data), and Markdown (documentation).

Frameworks and libraries: Next.js 15 (App Router, Route Handler for the API proxy, next/font), React 19, Tailwind CSS 4. No UI component library and no database — everything is hand-built CSS and React.

Runtime and tooling: Node.js, npm, TypeScript compiler (tsc) for type-checking, Vitest for unit tests (11 tests on the shift engine), Git and GitHub for version control, and the Next.js production build for optimization.

Deployment: Vercel (serverless hosting, automatic deploy from the GitHub master branch).

Browser APIs (no external assets): Web Audio API for all sound effects (oscillators and white noise — zero audio files), Web Speech API (speechSynthesis) for optional English narration, CSS @keyframes for the dust, light beam and cabin-shake effects.

Hardware: Only standard development laptops (Windows) — no servers, no GPUs, no sensors and no special hardware. The game itself needs no hardware beyond a web browser; it runs on desktop and mobile.

Verification tools: the Chrome DevTools Protocol (headless Edge) for automated end-to-end checks of the DOM, geometry and visuals, plus image/pixel analysis scripts to verify contrast, layout alignment and the "dirty vs. clean" state of the solar panels.

AI assistance: AI tools were used to help write and review code, styles and text, and to generate the guide's portrait image. This is disclosed in /creditos and in the README, and the interface contains no NASA logos or branding.

What factors did your team take into account?

- The audience (kids aged 7–12): one screen, no menus to explore, no reading-heavy instructions, short 60-second sessions, immediate visual and audio feedback, and consequences explained in a single sentence at the end of each shift.

- Data honesty: every figure on screen carries a provenance label distinguishing live NASA data, historical archives, reference values and fictional game rules. We never invent a measurement — if a source is unavailable, the game falls back to a clearly labelled archive snapshot instead of generating data.

- Live vs. historical clarity: only the DONKI space-weather feed is treated as live (refreshed at most once an hour); everything else is labelled as archive or reference so a historical record is never presented as current.

- API limits and reliability: a single server-side endpoint acts as a proxy and one-hour cache, keeping the API key out of the browser, avoiding CORS issues and staying inside the shared DEMO_KEY rate limit.

- Offline resilience: a local data snapshot means the game still works with no internet, which matters on conference Wi-Fi and for judges testing it later.

- Performance and cost: no audio or video files, a small first-load bundle (~113 kB), serverless deployment, and no database or account system, so it stays free to run and fast to load.

- Accessibility and inclusion: optional read-aloud narration, large touch targets, legible font sizes, support for both mobile and desktop, and respect for prefers-reduced-motion by disabling the storm, beam and shake animations.

- Legal and ethical compliance: no NASA logos, flags or institutional branding, explicit AI-generated content disclosure, and clear statements that the game is fiction and not a training, safety or forecasting tool.

- Code quality and verifiability: a pure, testable game engine separated from the UI, unit tests, type-checking, and automated browser checks before every release.

- Time and scope under hackathon constraints: a focused single-page architecture with reusable components, prioritising a polished 60-second loop over breadth, with the roadmap clearly separated from what is actually implemented.
